cells.quote: GTA programmes consistently reduce student anxiety and improve confidence, with learners reporting feeling calmer, more secure and better prepared for pelvic examinations following sessions (G1, G50, G51, G15, G56, G60, G82, G34, G16, G38). Confidence increased more for male students (G60) and was linked to previous sexual experience in both sexes (G1). While a few studies found no statistically significant differences compared to alternative teaching methods (G73, G24), overall, evidence supports a positive effect of GTA practice on reducing anxiety and enhancing confidence (G21, G36, G66).
cells.note: Scoping-review synthesis; evidence was frequently short-term and self-reported.

D.treatment: GTA teaching with immediate embodied feedback

O.outcome_detail: pelvic examination technique, procedural sequencing, psychomotor skill and competence

cells.quote: Across 27 studies, GTA training is associated with improvements in technical skill, knowledge and overall competence (Table 1). GTA-trained students outperform peers using manikins or clinical patients in pelvic examination technique, procedural sequencing, psychomotor skills and comfort during procedures (G65). Diagnostic ability, however, does not appear to differ from manikin-trained students (G65).
cells.note: The review reports mixed evidence across outcomes, including no apparent difference in diagnostic ability and mixed OSCE findings.

D.treatment: GTA-based teaching with structured immediate feedback
D.comparison: non-GTA teaching or alternative teaching methods

cells.quote: GTA involvement also enhances communication, professionalism and interpersonal skills. Students demonstrate greater awareness of patient comfort, autonomy and empathy. Further, structured GTA feedback improves supportive communication behaviours, including reassurance, rapport-building and attention to patient anxiety (G46, G47, G6, G51, G55, G21, G81, G25, G45, G53, G66). Although some long-term studies report no sustained differences compared to non-GTA groups (G46, G81), immediate benefits for patient-centred communication and professional development are consistently observed.
cells.note: The pooled literature includes immediate benefits and some studies without sustained long-term differences.

D.treatment: GTA teaching with real-time embodied feedback
D.comparison: manikin-based, faculty, standardised-patient or other teaching

O.outcome_detail: assessment validity when GTAs assess students they taught

cells.quote: Real-time, embodied feedback emerges as the key driver of GTA utility (Table 2). GTAs guide students' hands, confirm anatomy and signal discomfort within a supportive environment, enhancing technical competence, interpersonal sensitivity and confidence (G51, G47, G78, G25, G9, G24, G15, G45, G3). However, when GTAs assess students they have taught, familiarity may bias evaluation (Table 2), potentially inflating scores and limiting sustained skill acquisition (G47, G21, G25, G46). Tensions between the pedagogical value of direct GTA feedback and concerns about assessment validity when teaching and evaluation roles overlap have been reported (G75).
cells.note: The review identifies a risk to assessment validity but does not report a quantified comparative effect.
